paras: The lynching of Victor Mirando was the hanging of a youth of about sixteen, described as Mexican, by six masked men near Wilmington in Los Angeles County, California, in January 1881. Accused of assaulting a girl on her way to Sunday school, he was taken from the two men who had arrested him and hanged to a willow tree, and a coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of persons unknown. The Los Angeles Herald used the case to ask whether the county was returning to vigilance justice, and a wire dispatch carried it to papers across the country.

Mirando, about 16 or 17 and a resident of Florence, had been husking corn for a Mr. Bailey on the Cerritos rancho. According to the local account printed in the Herald and the Los Angeles Express, on Sunday, 9 January, he rode up to Mary Shaw, her sister Mamie and Emma Doyle as they walked to Sunday school from the Willows settlement and seized the youngest girl. That account said he then threw Mary Shaw down, dragged her into the willows and 'ravished' her, breaking her arm, while the wire said only that he 'attempted to outrage' one of the girls and broke her arm in the struggle.

A man named Teal and a young man named Garrison swore out a warrant and caught Mirando, still on horseback, near Wilmington late that afternoon; the Herald said he first denied the charge and then confessed. As the two were taking him toward Los Angeles, six masked men leveled shotguns at them and made them give up their prisoner. At first the masked men were thought to be friends attempting a rescue, but they took Mirando to Shaw's house, where the injured girl identified him, and then into the bush, where they hanged him.

Deputy Sheriff Hayes of Wilmington found the body on the morning of 11 January hanging from a willow tree on the ground used for a camp meeting the summer before, not far from where he had been captured.

Justice Johnson held an inquest, and the jury returned a verdict that Mirando had died by hanging at the hands of persons unknown to it. His step-father took charge of the remains, and Mary Shaw was reported in a high fever but expected to recover. No report of an arrest of the masked men appears in the coverage.

The Daily Los Angeles Herald printed the local story under 'Summary Punishment', calling Mirando 'the brute', and the Sacramento Record-Union reprinted the same text from the Los Angeles Express as 'Swift Punishment'. In an editorial the same day, the Herald said it deprecated lynch law but found this lynching 'not absolutely without palliation', blaming the 'immunity which crime has hitherto enjoyed' and courts and juries indifferent to violent crime. It predicted that the hanging would make rape 'very very unfashionable' in the county and closed by asking whether its people were ready to return to the old 'summary, if violent and unofficial' way of justice.

A Los Angeles dispatch dated 11 January ran on 12 January in the Memphis Daily Appeal as 'One Mexican Less', in the Chicago Tribune as 'LYNCHED', and in the Wheeling Register as 'A Fiend Of the Mexican Breed, Hanged by a Mob'. Versions of the same dispatch appeared in western papers such as the Eureka Daily Sentinel and the Las Vegas Morning Gazette and, in shortened form, in the Independent Statesman, the Delaware State Journal, the Washington Evening Star and Pennsylvania weeklies through 19 January. The briefest of these reduced the story to an attempted outrage followed by capture and hanging, without mentioning the masked men.

Accounts differed on the offense, the wire describing an attempted outrage and the local account a completed rape, and on his captors, whom the wire called 'a number of citizens' and the Herald named as Teal and Garrison acting on a warrant. His age appeared as about 16, 16 or 17, and, in the Chicago Tribune, 'about 10', and one condensed version said the masked men took him on Monday.

bases: Six masked men took Mirando from the two men who had arrested him and hanged him to a willow tree; a coroner's jury found he was hanged by persons unknown (A2, A4).

Six masked men seized Mirando at gunpoint from his captors, had him identified by the girl he was accused of assaulting, and hanged him (A2); the wire and the Herald's editorial call it a lynching for the alleged assault (A1, A4, A6). The victim was described as Mexican, not Black.
The Los Angeles wire dispatch (A4, A6, A7) and the local Herald/Express account (A2, A13) agree on the accusation, the seizure by masked men, the hanging and the coroner's verdict.

accounts.label: Los Angeles wire dispatch
accounts.gist: A Mexican of about sixteen attempted to outrage one of three girls and broke her arm; citizens captured him, masked men took him, and his body was found hanging near the place of capture.

accounts.label: Local account (Herald and Express)
accounts.gist: Teal and Garrison captured Mirando on a warrant; six masked men took him at gunpoint, had him identified by Mary Shaw at her father's house, and hanged him on a willow; it says he confessed after first denying.

accounts.label: Herald editorial
accounts.gist: Explained the lynching by the 'immunity which crime has hitherto enjoyed' and predicted vigilance committees if courts and juries did not act.

framing.detail: The Herald 'deprecate[d]' lynch law but called this one 'not absolutely without palliation' and said it would make rape 'very very unfashionable' in the county.
The local account, headed 'Summary Punishment', called him 'the brute' and treated his guilt as established; the Express reprint ran as 'Swift Punishment'.
Eastern papers ran the wire under 'One Mexican Less', 'LYNCHED' and 'A Fiend Of the Mexican Breed, Hanged by a Mob'.
